content: A back brace is a medical device specifically designed to restrict spinal motion in cases such as fractures or after spinal fusion surgeries. By limiting spinal movement, the brace promotes proper healing and reduces discomfort for the patient. There are two main types of back braces: 1. Rigid Braces: These are custom-molded plastic braces that fit snugly around the body and can restrict spinal motion by up to 50%. 2. Corset Braces: These are elastic braces that primarily limit forward spinal motion. They are often used to support the spine during activities that place stress on it, such as lifting heavy objects, or to assist in stabilizing spinal fusions. Bracing for Scoliosis Back braces are frequently prescribed for the treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, a condition where the spine develops an abnormal curvature during growth. These braces aim to halt the progression of the spinal curve. To protect the skin from irritation, patients typically wear a protective layer, such as a tank top or T-shirt, underneath the brace. Below are the most commonly used scoliosis braces: 1. Boston Brace: This is the most widely used scoliosis brace. It is made of molded plastic and is typically worn under clothing. While it can be removed for sports or physical activities, it is generally worn at all other times. 2. Cervico-Thoraco-Lumbo-Sacral Orthosis (Milwaukee Brace): Similar in design to the Boston brace, this device also includes a neck ring to provide support for the cervical spine. It is used for cases where additional support for the upper spine is required. 3. Charleston Brace: This brace is specifically designed to be worn during sleep. Studies have shown that wearing this brace for 8 hours at night is as effective as wearing other braces for 23 hours a day. It is most effective for spinal curvatures between 20 and 40 degrees, with the curve apex located below the shoulder blade. 4. SpineCor Brace: This is a flexible brace that allows for freedom of movement and is less noticeable under clothing. It is worn for 20 hours a day and is recommended for patients with a Cobb angle between 15 and 50 degrees. A bodysuit is typically worn underneath to enhance comfort. This brace is a newer design, and studies have shown positive outcomes after two years of use. It is not suitable for patients with a Risser score above 3, which indicates advanced skeletal maturity. 5. SPoRT Brace: This is a solid brace equipped with large pads, known as drives, that help elongate the spine. It also has stops to prevent incorrect movements that could worsen the spinal curve. A key advantage of this brace is that it does not restrict limb movement. It is typically worn for 23 hours a day. 6. Cheneau Brace: This brace is often used in conjunction with the Schroth Method, a specialized scoliosis rehabilitation program. A modified version, called the Lite Cheneau, replaces the bumped sections with open spaces for greater flexibility. Each of these braces is tailored to the specific needs of the patient and the characteristics of their spinal curvature. Proper use and adherence to the prescribed wearing schedule are critical for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes.
